summary: Describes how to use the AES cipher in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM) as an authenticated encryption method for TLS 1.2. GCM provides both confidentiality and data origin authentication and is efficient in hardware and software. The document defines the TLS cipher suites that use it, with RSA key exchange and Diffie-Hellman variants.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines TLS cipher suites that use AES-GCM to hide record contents and check that they were not changed. It also sets rules for choosing a unique nonce and for using the suites only with TLS 1.2 or later.

subtitle: Twelve TLS 1.2 cipher suites that use AES-GCM for encryption and authentication.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 defines authenticated encryption, but needed cipher suites using AES in Galois Counter Mode. This mode provides confidentiality and data origin authentication in one operation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines twelve suites using AES-GCM with RSA, Diffie-Hellman, or DSA-based key exchanges. Each record uses a 12-byte nonce made from a 4-byte salt and an 8-byte explicit value.
tldr.outcome: TLS 1.2 clients and servers can negotiate these AES-GCM suites, but must not use them with earlier TLS versions. RFC 5288 was updated by RFC 9325 and RFC 10015.

today: RFC 5288 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9325 and RFC 10015. Its cipher suites are defined for TLS 1.2 or later.

sections.title: AES-GCM as a TLS Cipher
sections.content:
RFC 5288 specifies how Transport Layer Security (TLS) uses the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) in Galois Counter Mode (GCM). GCM is authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD): it provides confidentiality and data origin authentication.

The RFC focuses on RSA, DSA, and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges. It says the mode can be efficiently implemented in hardware and software, and that elliptic-curve cipher suites are defined in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-GCM encrypts TLS records and checks their authenticity in one operation. This RFC defines the TLS cipher suites that use it.

sections.title: The Twelve Cipher Suites
sections.content:
The RFC defines twelve suites in six pairs. Each pair uses either a 128-bit or 256-bit AES key; the suite name also identifies a key-exchange method and a hash for the TLS pseudorandom function.

The key-exchange names are RSA, DHE_RSA, DH_RSA, DHE_DSS, DH_DSS, and DH_anon. The 128-bit suites use SHA-256 for the TLS PRF, and the 256-bit suites use SHA-384. Each suite uses a 128-bit authentication tag.

IANA assigned the suite values from 0x00,0x9C through 0x00,0xA7, in the order listed in the RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite list offers six key-exchange choices, each with a 128-bit and a 256-bit AES-GCM version. The suite name also determines which hash the TLS pseudorandom function uses.

sections.title: The GCM Nonce in Each Record
sections.content:
AES-GCM uses a nonce, a value that must not be repeated with the same key. RFC 5288 defines a 12-byte nonce with two parts: a 4-byte salt and an 8-byte nonce_explicit.

The salt comes from the TLS handshake and is not sent in each packet. The sender chooses the explicit part and carries it in every TLS record. It may use the 64-bit record sequence number for that value.

For each fixed key, every invocation of GCM encryption must use a distinct explicit nonce. Reusing one can significantly weaken security.
sections.plainLanguage: Each TLS record needs a nonce that is unique for its encryption key. The handshake supplies the salt, and the sender includes the explicit part in the record.

sections.title: The TLS Pseudorandom Function and Errors
sections.content:
The suite's suffix selects the hash used by the TLS pseudorandom function (PRF). A suite ending in _SHA256 uses the TLS PRF with SHA-256; a suite ending in _SHA384 uses it with SHA-384.

If any failure occurs while processing AES-GCM, an implementation must send the TLS alert bad_record_mac. The RFC does not define separate alerts for different GCM processing failures.
sections.plainLanguage: The suite name tells the peers which hash to use for the TLS PRF. If AES-GCM processing fails, the implementation reports the same TLS alert for every failure type.

sections.title: TLS 1.2 or Later Is Required
sections.content:
These cipher suites rely on authenticated encryption defined in TLS 1.2. They must not be negotiated with an earlier TLS version. A client must not offer them unless it also offers TLS 1.2 or later, and a server selecting an earlier version must not select one.

The RFC notes that a client cannot indicate support for TLS 1.2 without also permitting earlier versions. Therefore, if a server selects an earlier version with one of these suites, the client must send a fatal illegal_parameter alert.
sections.plainLanguage: These suites work only with TLS 1.2 or later. A client must stop if a server selects one while negotiating an earlier version.

sections.title: Avoiding Counter Reuse
sections.content:
The main additional security concern is reuse of a GCM counter value. The nonce construction is intended to prevent reuse, but implementations still need to ensure uniqueness under each key.

If a sender uses multiple encryption processors, each processor must use distinct explicit nonce values for a given key. The RFC recommends assigning each processor a fixed distinct part and combining it with a variable part that changes for each nonce. Those fixed parts must have equal lengths.
sections.plainLanguage: Two encryption operations must not reuse the same nonce with one key. When several processors encrypt records, each needs a way to produce distinct nonce values.
